title: 3-Read Friday #125
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's weekly 3-Read Friday curates three blog posts for teachers, each with a short editorial blurb. This issue pairs two classroom-technique pieces with one on memory and fluency. Bronwyn Jones argues that Cold Call is far more than picking a non-volunteer and cautions that a popular randomising shortcut can stop teachers developing the judgment the technique needs. Thahmina Begum uses Messi's scanning to argue that SLANT must be maintained thirty seconds into an explanation, setting out five moves to prevent, spot and correct drift. Dylan Kane argues that how repetition is structured matters as much as how much of it there is, drawing on activated long-term memory for maths and reading. The classroom-technique pieces dominate the issue, so it sits in Practice & Culture.
points: Barton frames Bronwyn Jones's piece as a case that Cold Call is a craft of teacher judgment, not a selection mechanism.
The Begum item extends SLANT beyond the opening of an explanation, with five moves to prevent, notice and correct drift.
Dylan Kane's post argues that poorly structured repetition can leave struggling students re-deriving the same facts indefinitely.
Taken together, the three picks stress deliberate teacher decisions during live instruction rather than reliance on routines or volume of practice.
Barton's blurbs preserve each author's central claim, so the issue works as a quick map of the week's most useful teaching writing.
quotes: I love deep dives into classroom techniques. Bronwyn argues that Cold Call is far more than picking a non-volunteer.
She also makes a provocative case against one popular shortcut, suggesting it may stop teachers from developing the very judgement the technique depends on.
Thahmina argues that if SLANT matters at the start of an explanation, it has to matter 30 seconds in too.
Drawing on research into how expert teachers scan the room, she sets out five simple moves to prevent, spot and correct the drift.
Dylan argues that how we structure repetition matters as much as how much of it we do. The wrong kind can leave struggling students re-deriving the same facts forever.
Drawing on a lesser-known idea from cognitive science, he shows how a few well-designed minutes can change that, in maths and reading alike.
